scenario: A tech company reports its overall hiring rates by gender across two departments: Engineering (high-selectivity) and HR (lower-selectivity). A journalist claims the data shows the company discriminates against women because the overall female hiring rate is lower.

data.description: Hiring rates by gender and department.

question: The overall hiring rate is 47% for men and 25.5% for women. Does this indicate gender discrimination? (a) Which gender has a higher hiring rate in Engineering? (b) Which gender has a higher hiring rate in HR? (c) Assuming applicants are equally likely to apply to either department (50/50), compute the corrected hiring rate for each gender and state which gender is hired at a higher rate.

ground_truth.explanation: Women are hired at a higher rate in both departments. The aggregate gap is entirely caused by women applying more to HR (lower-yield) and men applying more to Engineering (higher-yield). This is Simpson's paradox driven by application self-selection.

naive_answer: Men are hired at a higher rate overall (47% vs 25.5%), suggesting discrimination against women.
naive_trap: The aggregate comparison is confounded by department application rates. Women disproportionately apply to HR (900/1000 = 90%) while men disproportionately apply to Engineering (900/1000 = 90%). Within each department, women are hired at equal or higher rates.
